messages.subject: using STAN for prediction
parts:
I found from STAN manual the following code in the missing data section:

data {
        real y_obs[N];
}
parameters {
        real mu;
        real<lower=0> sigma;
        real y_mis;
}
 model {
        y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma);
        y_mis ~ normal(mu, sigma);
}

It seems that the same code will also work for predicting Y and my understanding is that for predicting something, we will need to declare it as parameters in STAN. Please advise if this is right.

I am trying to predict a binary outcome now and I found that if I do 
data {
        int<lower=0, upper=1> y_obs[N];
}
parameters {
        real mu;
        int<lower=0, upper=1> y_mis;
}
 model {
        y_obs ~ bernoulli_logit(mu);
        y_mis ~ bernoulli_logit(mu);
}

Then I got the error:
integer parameters or transformed parameters are not allowed;  found declared type int, parameter name=ypred
Problem with declaration.

Do you have suggestion for this?

I understand I may save the mu’s and predict y_mis outside of STAN afterwards. However, I am curious to get your advice whether all these can be done in STAN, which may allow me to predict using much more complicated models. 

The following is reply from Ben Goodrich (thanks a lot):

It is true that the Stan language does not allow you to declare an unknown parameter that is an integer. For binary data, it is pretty straightforward to introduce a continuous parameter such that the observable value is 1 if the continuous parameter is positive and the observable value is 0 if the continuous parameter is negative. This is very similar to a Gibbs sampler with binary outcomes and missing data, except that it is using NUTS instead of a Gibbs sampler. It would look something like this

data {
  int<lower=0> N_0; // number of observations with 0 as the outcome
  int<lower=0> N_1; // number of observations with 1 as the outcome
  int<lower=0> N_miss; // number of missing values on the outcome
}
parameters {
  real mu;
  vector<upper=0>[N_0] y_0;
  vector<lower=0>[N_1] y_1;
  vector[N_miss] y_miss;
}
model {
  for (i in 1:N_0) y_0[i] ~ logistic(mu, 1) T[,0];
  for (i in 1:N_1) y_1[i] ~ logistic(mu, 1) T[0,];
  y_miss ~ logistic(mu, 1);
  // prior on mu
}
generated quantities {
  int y_imp[N_miss];
  for (i in 1:N_miss) y_imp[i] = y_miss[i] > 0;
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] using STAN for prediction
parts:
> On Jan 7, 2017, at 9:27 PM, Chenguang Wang <chenguang...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I found from STAN manual the following code in the missing data section:
>
> data {
> real y_obs[N];
> }
> parameters {
> real mu;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> real y_mis;
> }
> model {
> y_obs ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> y_mis ~ normal(mu, sigma);
> }
>
> It seems that the same code will also work for predicting Y and my understanding is that for predicting something, we will need to declare it as parameters in STAN. Please advise if this is right.

You can look at the section of the manual on predictive modeling.
You can in general treat continuous predictions as parameters this
way. But if parameters are discrete or if you want more efficiency,
it's better to generate them in the generated quantities block because
then you get Monte Carlo inference (independent draws) instead of Markov
chain Monte Carlo (correlated draws) and Stan doesn't need to
calculate derivatives.

> I am trying to predict a binary outcome now and I found that if I do
> data {
> int<lower=0, upper=1> y_obs[N];
> }
> parameters {
> real mu;
> int<lower=0, upper=1> y_mis;
> }
> model {
> y_obs ~ bernoulli_logit(mu);
> y_mis ~ bernoulli_logit(mu);
> }
>
> Then I got the error:
> integer parameters or transformed parameters are not allowed; found declared type int, parameter name=ypred
> Problem with declaration.
>
> Do you have suggestion for this?

Yes, if it's discrete, it needs to g in generated quantities

generated quantities {
int<lower=0, upper=1> y_mis = bernoulli_logit_rng(mu);

> I understand I may save the mu’s and predict y_mis outside of STAN afterwards. However, I am curious to get your advice whether all these can be done in STAN, which may allow me to predict using much more complicated models.

Yes. See manual section:

8.16. Applications of Pseudorandom Number Generation

We need to add more about inference for posterior predictions.
There's more in some of the case studies you may find relevant.

- Bob
